title: DHCP Systems: Infrastructure & Leasing
subject: DHCP
description: Master the logic of dynamic addressing. These scenarios cover the lifecycle of an IP lease, from broadcast boundaries to failover synchronization.

tickets.title: "New DHCP server shows a red down arrow"
tickets.summary: The DHCP service is 'Running' in Services.msc, but the IPv4 node in the management console shows a red circle with a down arrow.
artifact: Event ID 1046: The DHCP service is not authorized to service clients.

triage.q: In a Windows Domain, what must happen before a DHCP server is allowed to lease IPs?
options: It must be Authorized in Active Directory

diagnosis.q: Why is the console icon red despite the service being 'On'?
options: Active Directory is blocking the server to prevent a 'Rogue' DHCP scenario
The server is out of RAM
Right-click the server in the console and select 'Authorize'

debrief.summary: Authorization prevents unauthorized servers from joining the network.
debrief.takeaway: You identified that a 'Running' service doesn't mean an 'Active' service. Because a bad DHCP server can break an entire network, Windows requires you to 'vouch' for the server in Active Directory. Once authorized, the red arrow turns green, and the server is trusted to start talking to clients.

tickets.title: "Wifi works on Floor 1, but Floor 2 gets 169.254 IPs"
tickets.summary: The DHCP server is on the Floor 1 subnet. Floor 2 clients are failing to get an IP address.
artifact: Router Config: IP Helper-Address is missing on the Floor 2 interface

triage.q: DHCP 'Discover' packets are broadcasts. How do they behave when they hit a router?
options: The router drops them by default
The router converts them to DNS queries

diagnosis.q: Why is Floor 2 isolated from the DHCP server?
options: The broadcast cannot cross the router 'wall' to reach the other subnet

fix.q: How do you bridge the connection?
options: Configure an 'IP Helper-Address' (Relay Agent) on the router

debrief.summary: Routers act as barriers for broadcast traffic.
debrief.takeaway: You realized the server was working fine, but the 'request' was trapped on the second floor. Since routers stop broadcasts to keep network noise low, you had to give the router a 'forwarding address' (IP Helper) to act as a courier for those requests.

tickets.title: "Console is reporting BAD_ADDRESS conflicts"
tickets.summary: The address lease list is filling up with 'BAD_ADDRESS' entries, and users report 'IP Conflict' popups.
artifact: Context: A tech recently installed 3 networked time-clocks with static IPs.

triage.q: What does 'BAD_ADDRESS' indicate in the DHCP console?
options: The server attempted to offer an IP but found someone was already using it
Static IPs were set within the range the DHCP server is trying to lease out
The lease time is too long

fix.q: How do you stop the server from trying to use those IPs?
options: Create an 'Exclusion Range' for the static IPs

debrief.summary: Exclusions prevent IP collisions between static and dynamic devices.
debrief.takeaway: The server actually protected the network by 'pinging' the IP first and seeing someone else answered. By creating an Exclusion, you told the server to stop touching those specific IPs, ending the 'tug-of-war' between the new time-clocks and the DHCP pool.

tickets.title: "Guest Wi-Fi says 'No IP addresses available'"
tickets.summary: The Guest Wi-Fi scope is 100% full. Most guests only stay for a few hours, yet the pool never empties.

triage.q: What happens to an IP lease when a guest leaves the building?
options: It stays 'reserved' for that guest until the lease duration expires
It returns to the pool immediately

diagnosis.q: Why is the scope exhausted even though the lobby is empty?
options: The 8-day lease is holding onto IPs for people who aren't there anymore

fix.q: What is the best adjustment for high-turnover areas?
options: Shorten the lease duration to 2 or 4 hours

debrief.summary: Lease duration controls how quickly the server recycles IPs.
debrief.takeaway: You identified that the IPs weren't 'missing'; they were just 'trapped' by a long lease. By shortening the duration, you allow the server to 'clean up' and reclaim addresses much faster, making a small pool of IPs work for hundreds of different guests throughout the week.

tickets.title: "Secondary DHCP server is giving out old DNS info"
tickets.summary: You updated the DNS settings on the Primary server, but the Failover partner is still handing out the old IPs.
artifact: Sync Status: Leases are syncing, but options are not.

triage.q: Do configuration changes (Options) sync automatically in a failover pair?
options: No, they must be manually replicated

diagnosis.q: Why is the partner out of sync?
options: The settings change hasn't been 'replicated' to the partner server

fix.q: How do you push the new config?
options: Right-click the scope and select 'Replicate Scope'

debrief.summary: Failover pairs sync leases automatically, but configuration requires a manual push.
debrief.takeaway: You discovered that 'Leases' (who has what) and 'Rules' (DNS/Gateway) are handled differently. Manually triggering replication ensures that no matter which server answers the client, they get the same up-to-date instructions.

tickets.title: "Users have an IP but 'No Internet' status"
tickets.summary: Running `ipconfig /all` shows a valid IP and Subnet, but the 'Default Gateway' line is completely blank.
artifact: Connectivity: Internal ping works, external ping fails

triage.q: Which DHCP Option provides the 'exit route' (Default Gateway) for a subnet?

diagnosis.q: Why is the gateway missing on the clients?
options: The DHCP server isn't configured to send Option 003
The user is on a static IP
Add Option 003 to the Scope Options with the Router's IP

debrief.summary: DHCP is a configuration engine for the whole network stack.
debrief.takeaway: You realized that an IP address alone is like having a house with no driveway—you can't leave. By adding Option 003, you provided the necessary 'exit route' the computers needed to reach the internet, proving DHCP does much more than just name-tagging.

tickets.title: "The NAS is not getting its reserved .200 address"
tickets.summary: A storage device has a reservation for 10.0.0.200, but it keeps appearing with a random IP like .105.

triage.q: What unique hardware ID does DHCP use to match a reservation to a device?

options: The MAC address in the reservation entry has a typo
Update the reservation with the correct MAC address

debrief.summary: Reservations rely on exact hardware matches.
debrief.takeaway: You found the typo! DHCP logic is strict: if the hardware ID (MAC) doesn't match perfectly, the server doesn't recognize the device as 'special.' Correcting the MAC ensures the server recognizes the NAS and grants it the reserved IP every time.

tickets.title: "Lease durations changed to 1 hour after Server A went down"
tickets.summary: With Server A offline, Server B is handling all requests, but users notice their leases expire every 60 minutes.

triage.q: In a failover relationship, what does 'MCLT' represent?
options: The temporary lease time a secondary server gives out during an outage
The maximum number of clients allowed

diagnosis.q: Why are the leases so short during the outage?
options: The secondary server uses the MCLT 'safety' duration until it can confirm the primary is gone for good

fix.q: Is this a bug or normal behavior?

debrief.summary: MCLT is a protective timer during server transitions.
debrief.takeaway: You discovered the 'fail-safe.' The secondary server only gives out short 1-hour leases so it doesn't accidentally conflict with the primary server later. It's the server's way of saying, 'I'll help you for now, but check back soon in case the boss wakes up!'

tickets.title: "Computer names aren't showing up in DNS anymore"
tickets.summary: DHCP is leasing IPs correctly, but internal name resolution is failing for new laptops.
artifact: DHCP Properties -> DNS Tab: 'Dynamically update DNS' is unchecked
DNS Console: Missing records for new 'LAPTOP-' names

triage.q: Where is the automated 'partnership' between DHCP and DNS configured?
options: The DNS Tab in DHCP Server Properties

diagnosis.q: Why is the DNS phonebook out of date?
options: DHCP hasn't been told to 'tell' DNS when it hands out a new lease
Enable 'Dynamically update DNS records' in DHCP

debrief.summary: DHCP and DNS must work together to keep the network organized.
debrief.takeaway: You bridged the communication gap. When DHCP hands out an IP, it should immediately 'ring up' the DNS server to update the records. Turning this on ensures your network 'phonebook' stays accurate automatically as devices come and go.

tickets.title: "The DHCP service won't start - Error 1067"
tickets.summary: The DHCP service crashes immediately on startup. Event logs point to a database error.
artifact: Event Log: 'The DHCP service failed to initialize the database'

triage.q: Where does Windows store the physical DHCP lease database?

options: The physical database file is corrupted and cannot be read

fix.q: How do you recover without rebuilding from scratch?
options: Use the 'Restore' command to pull from the automatic backup folder

debrief.summary: DHCP relies on a local database file that can occasionally fail.
debrief.takeaway: You treated DHCP like what it actually is—a database application. When the file breaks, the service can't start. Using the Restore feature points the service to a healthy backup copy, bringing your scopes and leases back to life in seconds.
